title: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 139. Scope: digit sequences of square roots of non-square integers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Digits can be generated accurately for many examples and examined with standard methods. Existing computation cannot cover every integer or establish asymptotic randomness, so the universal statement is only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample non-square integers under declared schemes, compute long expansions of their square roots in specified bases, and apply a fixed battery of randomness tests. Counterexamples refute the universal appearance claim, while passing samples support only bounded ranges and tests.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Random appearance depends on base, sample length, and test.

Every non-square integer is an infinite scope.

Normality is unknown for individual algebraic irrationals.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.42
discriminating power: 0.65
data existence: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.68
analysis feasibility: 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Any particular square root is computable to enormous precision, and a single patterned expansion would refute the claim that every non-square has random-looking digits. A large sample can be checked in weeks and would resolve the claim on that sample. It would not reach every non-square integer or the infinite tail of each expansion, so the universal statement stays partly open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For a large set of non-square integers, compute long digit prefixes of the square root in several bases and run randomness tests. One systematic digit pattern would refute the universal claim; clean results on the sample support it only inside that sample and those lengths.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim quantifies over every non-square and every digit position, which no finite sample covers.

Normality of specific square roots is open, so tests speak only to appearance.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.6
data existence: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.75
